text: Imagine you are signing into your favorite music app, and you type your password incorrectly.
You don't want this system to let you in because your guess was close, or because your spelling was creative.
You want it to follow a strict, unforgiving condition.
Deny access unless the text matches exactly.
That rigid condition forms the foundation of all traditional, non-AI software.
A calculator executes exact mathematical operations, and a spreadsheet applies rigid formulas to your data.
And for every one of those operations, a human programmer had to sit down and manually write the instructions.
This chart illustrates exactly what those rules look like.
A user enters a password.
If the password matches, the logic follows the green path and opens the app.
Otherwise, it follows the red path and shows an error message.
Written rules return the same result every time.
Traditional software excels when a task requires absolute mathematical certainty.
If your input deviates even slightly from the pre-written instructions, the process simply stops.
Suppose you and your friends hand-wrote a playlist for a party.
That physical piece of paper is a mess of crossed-out ideas,
with arrows pointing to replacement songs, shorthand abbreviations, and jokes written in the margins.
It is mathematically impossible for a programmer to write a separate,
explicit rule to account for every unique scribble, arrow, and scratch through on that page.
This specific limitation is exactly what large language models, or LLMs, are designed to solve.
An LLM learns patterns during training.
Because the AI relies on those broad patterns rather than rigid code,
it looks at your messy notebook paper and deciphers your intent,
extracting the real songs without needing pre-written instructions for every abbreviation.
AI is still software.
People still write the code to train and run it.
The difference is, they no longer write a separate rule for every single possible request.
When human information stops being perfectly clean and predictable,
software must transition from following strict rules to recognizing complex patterns.
This graphic shows a helpful analogy.
Rule-based software is a cooking robot following a recipe,
achieving the exact same result every time.
But AI is a chef, recognizing patterns in ingredients and methods.
The chef doesn't need a recipe.
To understand why the chef matters, look at how software handles information.
If you calculate a GPA by putting grades and credits into spreadsheet columns,
you are using structured data.
It is organized into consistent fields.
But suppose you take a picture while visiting a college and want to know the names of the dorms.
That is unstructured data.
The visual information is chaotic and completely lacks consistent fields.
AI can apply its learned patterns to that unstructured photograph.
It evaluates the shape of the architecture, reads visible signage,
and processes the surrounding layout to identify the specific dorm buildings.
AI's true utility lies in its ability to extract actionable meaning
from the chaotic, unstructured data that dominates the real world.
Relying on learned patterns gives AI incredible flexibility.
But this foundation creates a significant trade-off.
A written password check is easy to inspect and entirely predictable.
And AI's pattern-based responses can be highly unpredictable.
If you give an AI that messy, handwritten playlist,
it might completely misinterpret a pointing arrow
and confidently add a crossed-out song to your cue.
Or, analyzing that college campus photo,
it might misread a signpost and give you the completely wrong name for a dorm building.
It might look great, but still have mistakes.
Different jobs need different tools.
Choose the tool that fits the work.
Technological competence requires you to understand the limitations of both systems,
allowing you to deploy the right logic to solve the right problem.
